answer_text:
Let

\[
K=F_p(X,Y), \qquad L=F_p(X^p,Y^p).
\]

Set \(A=X^p\) and \(B=Y^p\), so \(L=F_p(A,B)\).

**Upper bound.**  
Since \(X^p=A\in L\), \(X\) is algebraic over \(L\) of degree at most \(p\). Similarly, \(Y^p=B\in L\), so \(Y\) is algebraic over \(L(X)\) of degree at most \(p\). Thus by the tower law,

\[
[K:L]=[F_p(X,Y):F_p(X^p,Y^p)]\le p^2.
\]

**Lower bound.**  
Consider \(R=F_p[X,Y]\) and \(S=F_p[A,B]=F_p[X^p,Y^p]\). As an \(S\)-module, \(R\) has basis

\[
\{X^iY^j:0\le i,j\le p-1\},
\]

since every monomial \(X^mY^n\) can be uniquely written as

\[
A^aB^bX^iY^j
\]

with \(0\le i,j\le p-1\).

Now suppose a linear relation over \(L\) holds:

\[
\sum_{i,j=0}^{p-1} \lambda_{ij}X^iY^j=0,
\qquad \lambda_{ij}\in L.
\]

Clearing denominators gives a nontrivial \(S\)-linear relation among the same monomials in \(R\), which is impossible because they form an \(S\)-basis. Hence the \(p^2\) elements \(X^iY^j\) are linearly independent over \(L\), so

\[
[K:L]\ge p^2.
\]

Combining the bounds gives

\[
[K:L]=p^2.
\]

\[
\boxed{p^2}
\]
